title: Pairwise block accumulation and scaled-softmax test harness
content:
Purpose and scope:

This working note documents a focused investigation into two related numeric stability problems we’ve been hitting in the serving runtime with mixed-precision execution: (1) noisy / NaN failures caused by long accumulation chains during attention and feed-forward reductions when accumulators are low precision, and (2) magnitude collapse or overflow in the softmax step when logits come from heterogeneous sources (fresh compute vs KV cache). The goal is to propose practical kernel-level and scheduler-level mitigations that trade a small amount of latency for big improvements in determinism and failure rate.

Background / root causes (hypotheses):

1) Accumulation error amplification: when we sum many FP16 contributions (e.g. long sequence attention or fused linear reductions across large batch x seq_len), the rounding error can bias results and occasionally produce denorms/NaNs once later layers or normalization amplify the error. The dominant factors are sequence length, head dimension, and whether accumulation happens in FP16 vs FP32.

2) Softmax scaling mismatch: our KV cache stores keys and values produced under an earlier scaling regime or quantization path. When we mix cached KV with newly computed queries, logits' dynamic range can change substantially. In FP16 this can lead to very large exponents (overflow) or too-small exponents (underflow) before softmax normalization, producing near-0/NaN attention scores.

3) Scheduler amplification: our batching/scheduling often coalesces many requests and increases the effective length of reduction operations inside a single kernel launch, increasing the number of terms accumulated and worsening rounding error. Micro-batching or coalescing across heterogeneous request shapes can exacerbate numeric instability.

Prior mitigations tried (quick summary):

- Force accumulation in FP32 for all reductions: stable but ~20–45% slower and increases memory pressure (already captured in prior notes).
- Stochastic rounding: promising in some microbenchmarks but costly and non-deterministic; implementation complexity high on current kernel stack.
- Per-layer fixed scaling factor applied at softmax input: mitigates some cases but brittle when dynamic range changes at runtime (cache vs fresh).

New proposal: pairwise-block accumulation + adaptive scaled-softmax heuristic

A. Pairwise-block accumulation (PBA)
- Idea: Do pairwise summation in blocks (tree-reduction style) inside kernels instead of linear accumulation. Within each block we also keep an intermediate accumulator in higher precision (FP32 or bfloat16 with FP32 accumulation emulation).
- Implementation sketch for attention reductions and linear reductions:
  - split reduction axis into blocks of size B (tunable, default 64–256 depending on head dim and hardware warp size)
  - within each block perform pairwise summation: sum pairs, then sum results pairwise (balanced tree) to reduce rounding bias
  - accumulate block results into an FP32 accumulator (optionally bfloat16 with pairwise correction)
  - output cast down to target precision only at the end
- Expected benefits: reduces rounding bias from O(n) to O(log n) in the number of terms, which significantly reduces the probability of denorm/NaN cascades when later ops amplify small errors.
- Cost: minimal extra shuffles inside registers/SM memory, small extra latency relative to pure FP16 linear accumulation; can be implemented as an alternative kernel path enabled by flag.

B. Adaptive scaled-softmax heuristic (ASSH)
- Idea: Before softmax we compute a cheap statistics probe of logits' range (max, min, approximate variance) per attention head; use this to pick one of three paths:
  - nominal path: single-pass FP16 softmax with small constant scale s=1.0 when range in safe band
  - shifted-path: subtract a per-head offset (max) and apply a dynamic multiplier if variance is low (prevents underflow)
  - FP32 fallback: re-run softmax in FP32 only for heads where probe indicates overflow/underflow risk or NaNs observed
- For KV cache interaction: store a small per-layer/per-head scaling tag alongside KV entries (one fp8/bf16 or int8 metadata) that indicates the scale used during KV creation; when reusing KV, combine saved scale with probe to detect dangerous mismatches. This avoids blind mixing of differently scaled tensors.
- Implementation detail: the probe should be ~O(1) extra work (per head max and a quick top-k sample) and avoid full FP32 conversion of the entire tensor. On GPUs this can be fused with existing reductions.

Interaction with scheduler and kernel selection:

- The scheduler should expose a knob "numeric_precision_budget" per route/customer that indicates how much extra computation we can spend on FP32 fallbacks. The optimizer will then select kernels:
  - high-throughput paths: prefer PBA in FP16 accumulators with scaled-softmax nominal path
  - conservative paths: prefer full-FP32 reductions for critical customers or when sequence length > threshold
- A scheduling heuristic: limit the maximum contiguous reduction length fused into a single kernel across coalesced requests. If coalescing would create a reduction length > L_max (tunable), split into micro-batches so each kernel operates on smaller reductions, thereby reducing accumulation depth. This is a scheduling-level mitigation that reduces need for expensive FP32 work.

KV cache specific proposals:

1) Per-entry scale metadata: when writing KV to cache, compute a cheap head-wise scale factor and store it with the cache. On read, compare cached scales with current compute scales; if mismatch > epsilon, trigger ASSH shifted-path or FP32 fallback for that head.

2) Cache re-normalization pass: periodically (low priority background) rescale cached KV entries to match the current model scaling regime. This is async and best-effort; helps long-lived caches in interactive sessions.

Microbench and regression test plan (test harness):

- Build a targeted harness for synthetic worst-case patterns:
  - alternating large/small logits, monotonic sequences, and adversarial patterns that maximize exponent spread
  - long sequence lengths (512, 1024, 2048) with large head dims
  - mixed cache/fresh inputs with controlled scale mismatches (store a KV with scale s=2.0 and test with s=0.5 queries etc.)
- Metrics to collect: per-head NaN rate, per-head max/min logits, softmax entropy, attention mass concentration, end-to-end normalized difference vs FP32 baseline (L1/Linf), performance overhead (ns/token)
- CI integration: add a nightly job that runs 3-5 seed variations of the adversarial harness across representative GPUs (A100, H100, T4) and flags regressions when NaN_rate > threshold or L1_delta > threshold. Store failing traces in an artifact bucket for debuggability.

Small experimental results (local runs on A100 dev box):

- Baseline (FP16 linear accumulation + plain softmax): NaN_rate ~ 0.9% on adversarial harness with seq_len=1024, head_dim=128, mixed cache scales
- With PBA enabled (blocks=128, FP32 block accumulator): NaN_rate dropped to 0.03%; average per-request latency increased +6%
- With ASSH enabled (probe + per-head shift + FP32 fallback on flagged heads): NaN_rate ~ 0.01%; extra average latency +9% but 95th percentile tail reduced by ~18% (fewer catastrophic failures)
- Combined PBA + ASSH: NaN_rate indistinguishable from zero on 50-run sample; avg latency +11% vs baseline but tail p99 latency reduced by ~25% because we avoid re-running requests after NaN detection.

Open questions and follow-ups:

- Optimal block size B per hardware and per head_dim: we need a small sweep matrix (B in {32,64,128,256} x head_dim in {64,128,256}) across GPUs to pick smart defaults.
- Cost of tracking per-entry KV scale metadata vs cache memory pressure: metadata is small (one fp16 per head) but we need to quantify effect on cache storage and eviction policies.
- Determinism vs stochastic rounding: should PBA be combined with low-cost compensated summation (Kahan) for a deterministic path? Kahan has branches and extra ops; possibly heavy in some kernels.
- Edge-case of very small models where FP32 fallback might be cheaper than PBA overhead – add autotuner.

Action items (concrete next steps):

- (Ethan) Prototype pairwise-block accumulation kernel in runtime/kernels/attention_pba.cu, default disabled behind runtime flag; aim for microbench by end of sprint (2 weeks).
- (Aisha) Add ASSH probe and per-head scale tag to KV cache write path and read path; add unit tests that simulate scale mismatch.
- (Marcel) Add adversarial harness to runtime-tests/numeric_harness with config parametrization and CI job template.
- (Lina) Run block-size sweep across A100/H100 and produce a short recommendation doc with perf/accuracy trade-offs.
- Create a short RFC with measured numbers and recommended default runtime flag settings; target product review in three weeks.

Appendix: quick pseudocode (attention reduction with PBA):

// high-level, simplified:
// inputs: matrix M of shape [batch, heads, seq_len, head_dim]
for each batch, head:
  for i in 0..seq_len step B:
    block = M[:, i:i+B, :]
    // pairwise tree reduction inside block into fp32 accumulator
    partial = pairwise_sum_tree(block, accum_type=FP32)
    global_accum = global_accum + partial  // in FP32
  out = cast(global_accum, target_type)

Notes: pairwise_sum_tree should be register-friendly; on CUDA targets we should implement with warp-shuffle and block-shuffle primitives to avoid extra shared memory when possible.

If you want, I can convert this into a short RFC-style doc (one-pager + perf table) or generate the kernel microbench scripts next.
